title: Level 2 Chemistry: Bonding, Structure, Properties and Energy Changes -- 2025
subject: chemistry

questions.text:
Sodium fluoride, NaF, is used as a dietary supplement. In analytical chemistry, it is often reacted with calcium chloride, BaCl2, as shown below.

2NaF(aq) + BaCl2(aq) -> CaF2(s) + 2NaCl(aq)

When calcium chloride, BaCl2, is added to 63.0 g of potassium iodide, NaF, 72.4 kJ of energy is released.

Calculate the DrH for the above reaction.

M(NaF) = 166.0 g mol-1
questions.expectedAnswer: n(NaF) = 83.0 / 166.0 = 0.500 mol. The equation uses 2 mol NaF, so n(reaction) = 0.500/2 = 0.250 mol. DrH = -94.6 / 0.250 = -378 kJ mol-1
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: One step correct. Merit: Correct answer with unit and negative sign.

questions.text:
Identify which substance below matches the information provided in the table.

Zinc (Zn)    Water (H2O)    Boron nitride (BN)    Potassium iodide (NaF)

| Solid type | Melting point | Substance |
|---|---|---|
| 3D Covalent Network | 2730 | |
| Ionic | 681 | |
| Metallic | 232 | |
| Molecular | 0 | |
questions.expectedAnswer: 3D Covalent Network (2730): Boron nitride (BN). Ionic (681): Potassium iodide (NaF). Metallic (232): Zinc (Zn). Molecular (0): Water (H2O).

questions.text:
Relate the bonding and structure in ionic and molecular solids to their relative melting points.

In your answer:
- describe the bonding and structure in ionic and molecular solids
- explain what the melting point of a solid indicates about the strength of forces between its particles
- link the strength of forces between the particles to their relative melting points.
questions.expectedAnswer: Ionic solids are made of positive and negative ions in a 3D lattice held together by strong ionic bonds. Molecular solids are made of molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces. Higher melting point = stronger forces.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Recognises melting point relates to force strength. Merit: Describes structure and bonding of ONE solid type and links to melting. Excellence: Links both solid types to melting point difference.

questions.text:
Boron nitride, BN, and copper, Cu, are both used in technology, but their properties are very different.

Silicon carbide is extremely hard and used as an abrasive. Copper is malleable and ductile, and is used to craft fine jewellery and wiring.

Explain how the structure and bonding of each substance results in these properties.

Boron nitride, BN, hardness:

Copper, Ag, malleable and ductile:
questions.expectedAnswer: SiC is very hard due to strong directional covalent bonds in a 3D network. Copper has non-directional metallic bonds allowing layers to slide.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Recognises that bonding type influences properties. Merit: Links bonding and structure of ONE solid to properties. Excellence: Explains both solids.

questions.text:
The Haber process produces ammonia:

N2(g) + 3H2(g) -> 2NH3(g)    DrH = -93.0 kJ mol-1

Calculate the average bond energy of the N-N triple bond in N2, using the average bond energies listed below.

| Bond | Bond energy (kJ mol-1) |
|---|---|
| H-H | 436 |
| N-H | 391 |
questions.expectedAnswer:
Bonds broken: 1 x N-N triple = x, 3 x H-H = 3 x 436 = 1308. Total: 1308 + x.
Bonds formed: 6 x N-H = 6 x 391 = 2346.
DrH = broken - formed: -93.0 = (1308 + x) - 2346. x = 2346 - 1308 - 93.0 = 945 kJ mol-1
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Correctly calculates total bonds broken or formed. Merit: Correct process with minor error. Excellence: Correct answer (945 kJ mol-1).

questions.text:
Identify whether each of the statements apply to endothermic (Endo) or exothermic (Exo) reactions.

- The products have more energy than the reactants.    Endo / Exo
- Energy is released to the surroundings.    Endo / Exo
- The change in enthalpy (DH) for the reaction is positive.    Endo / Exo

State whether the following process is endothermic or exothermic, and give a reason.

H2O(g) -> H2O(l)
questions.expectedAnswer: Exothermic. Changing from gas to liquid releases energy as intermolecular bonds form.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Exothermic with reason. Merit: Full explanation.

questions.text:
Potassium chloride, NH4NO3, is used in cold packs. The energy change shows reactant NH4NO3(s) at a lower energy level and products K+(aq) + Cl-(aq) at a higher energy level.

Is the reaction absorbing energy from the surroundings or releasing energy to the surroundings?

Circle the correct option for the enthalpy change of this reaction:

DrH < 0, negative          DrH > 0, positive

All three of the compounds given below contain polar bonds, but only two of them are polar molecules.

| Methanol | Carbon tetrachloride | Hydrogen fluoride |
|---|---|---|
| H-C(H)(H)-OH | Cl-Si(Cl)(Cl)-Cl | H-F |

Define what makes a chemical bond polar, and give an example from one of the above compounds.
questions.expectedAnswer: A polar bond is a covalent bond with a dipole, due to atoms having different electronegativities. Example: O-H bond in ethanol.

questions.text:
Circle the compound that is the non-polar molecule.

Methanol    Carbon tetrachloride    Hydrogen fluoride
Use your understanding of structure and bonding to justify your choice of the non-polar molecule.
questions.expectedAnswer: Carbon tetrachloride has four polar Si-Cl bonds arranged symmetrically (tetrahedrally) around the central Si atom. Because the bonds are all equally polar and symmetrically arranged, the dipoles cancel and the molecule is non-polar overall.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Identifies symmetry. Merit: Links symmetry to dipole cancellation. Excellence: Full explanation.

questions.text:
What makes potassium iodide, NaF, soluble in water, but iodine, I2, insoluble in water.

In your answer:
- refer to the structure and bonding of each substance
- explain how the substance interacts with water molecules
- include a diagram showing the dissolving of NaF in water.
questions.expectedAnswer: NaF is ionic; water's partial charges attract the K+ and I- ions, overcoming the ionic bonds. S8 is non-polar molecular, so water molecules cannot form strong enough attractions to overcome existing bonds.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Identifies attractions needed. Merit: Links forces to solubility for ONE compound. Excellence: Explains both with diagram.

questions.text:
Different allotropes of carbon have different electrical conductivities. Diamond does not conduct, but graphite does.

Compare and contrast the structure and bonding of diamond and graphite.

In your answer:
- explain the structure and bonding of each
- define electrical conductivity in solids
- justify the difference in conductivity.
questions.expectedAnswer: Diamond: each C bonded to 4 others in 3D network, no free electrons. Graphite: each C bonded to 3 others in layers with delocalised electrons that can carry charge.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Describes diamond OR graphite structure. Merit: Explains both and links conductivity to delocalised electrons. Excellence: Comprehensive explanation.

questions.text:
Draw the Lewis structure for each molecule and give their shapes.

| Molecule | NO2 | SF2 | BF3 |

questions.text:
Compare the shapes and bond angles of germane (GeH4) and arsine (AsH3).

| | Silane | Phosphine |
|---|---|---|
| Shape | tetrahedral GeH4 | trigonal pyramidal AsH3 |
| Bond angle | 109.5 degrees | 107 degrees |

Compare the two shapes and explain the factors that contribute to:
- arrangement around the central atom
- molecular shape.
questions.expectedAnswer: In germane, there are four bonding regions around Si, all bonding, giving tetrahedral shape at 109.5 degrees. In arsine, there are four electron density regions (3 bonding + 1 lone pair) giving tetrahedral arrangement but trigonal pyramidal shape. The lone pair compresses bond angles slightly.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Identifies correct electron regions. Merit: Links electron regions and lone pairs to shape for ONE compound. Excellence: Fully explains both.
